summary.title: 20 Things I've Learned in my 20 Years as a Software Engineer
summary.one_liner: A veteran engineer's list of 20 contextual lessons on software design, teams, process, and hiring, drawn from small startups, large consulting work, and running a small firm.
takeaways: Most software effort is wasted when teams build the wrong thing; design is largely about listening to users.
Avoid 0.1x programmers rather than chasing mythical 10x programmers, and prefer reusing existing tools over reinventing them.
Keep processes lean, give teams ownership of outcomes, and iterate in small chunks instead of building the biggest system up front.
Treat your data as the most durable asset, and favor long-lived, proven technologies unless there is a strong reason to replace them.
Interviews are poor predictors of team fit; advice of any kind needs context before it applies.
summary.summary: The post is a numbered list of 20 lessons the author collected over two decades of software work, from small startups and large enterprises to running a 25-person consultancy. It opens with a caveat that most advice is contextual and the author states the context their own views come from: small lean teams, working software over specific tools, and engineer productivity. Each point is a short essay with personal anecdotes and opinions rather than data or code. Topics range from design and user empathy to process, hiring, data integrity, and building smaller systems.
